title: I Took the Community Compost-Tumbler Hours to the Chair Who Left My Numbered Batch

parts.text: I stepped into bin three at 8:08 a.m. and chair Ned was already using my numbered batch. The board said: ONE BATCH. FOURTEEN DAYS. BINS STAY WITH THE BOOKING. I was thirty-eight, garden steward, holding a clipboard that listed our turn. Ned shrugged. "Chairs keep the pile." I photographed the board, the booking, and his greens in my tumbler. Then I asked for the tumbler hours. At 8:16 the garden desk pinged why Ned's greens sat in our tumbler. I kept my voice indoor and let the timestamp talk. A paper policy is only paper until someone treats it like a clock.
parts.cliffhanger_hint: The garden desk can see Ned's greens in bin three during our turn.

social.video_title: He left his greens in my numbered tumbler — Part 1/2
social.description: Compost tumbler, a chair in my bin, a fourteen-day clock he posted. I logged the greens. Would you have asked for the tumbler hours?

parts.text: Ned called it browns until the desk asked for the photo. I printed the ticket, the board, and the tumbler still. The batch went back to my numbered tag. Ned ran a slot of their own and told the next chair atmosphere was always about optics. Optics is a word people use when a booking exists. Policy now has a second line: CHAIRS DO NOT KEEP THE PILE. I keep our turn on a labeled card. Ned brown-bags his greens. The tumbler finally looks like a booking, not a loan. The rule looks ordinary now, which is the whole point.

social.video_title: Chairs do not keep the pile — Part 2/2
social.description: Tumbler hours, numbered batch, and a second line on the board. Were browns ever our turn?
